aliases: Kanchanjangha Tea Estate and Research Centre
processing: Organic orthodox-style teas from smallholder land: black tea, with green, white and oolong lots also sold.
harvest_season: Little is documented on prized pickings here; as elsewhere in the eastern Nepali hills, spring and autumn lots are usually sought.
appearance_dry: Twisted dark leaf, often with lighter tips, as is usual for Nepali orthodox tea.
appearance_liquor: Clear amber, as is usual for Nepali orthodox black tea.
appearance_wet: Mixed coppery-brown leaf, as is usual for a Himalayan orthodox tea.
taste_profile: Few specific tasting records exist for the black tea; expect the fragrant, medium-bodied Himalayan style, close to Darjeeling, with fruit or flowers depending on the flush.

brewing.notes: A general starting point for Himalayan orthodox tea. Spring lots want cooler water and a watchful eye.

vintage_note: Sold through organic importers by type and often by lot, with the harvest year stated by the better sellers. As with other Nepali orthodox teas, the current year's lot is the one to buy, and fresh is better than aged.
description:
Kanchanjangha Tea Estate sits in Panchthar in eastern Nepal, between about 1,300 and 1,800 metres, just north of Ilam. What sets it apart is its model: smallholders pooled their land and became co-owners.

It is described as Nepal's first certified organic tea garden, and today it sells black tea plus green, white and oolong lots.

The black tea has few detailed tasting records. Expect the Himalayan style, and brew it the way you would a Darjeeling, with slightly cooler water.

Look for it among organic importers, where a named lot and year are the things to check. If you like it, compare it with the Dhankuta gardens to the west.
history:
Accounts agree on the core story and differ on the date. A group of about 100 local farmers joined their land in a cooperative venture, with the politician and cooperative founder Dipak Prakash Baskota as a founder. The start is given as 1980 or 1984.

The estate grew into a cooperative in which farmers hold a stake. One seller reports more than 150 farmers directly involved and about 400 more indirectly, along with free housing and help with food, healthcare and education, though those claims come from the trade itself.
